name: Adam Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, independent of AI firms, employers, unions, parties and government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What happens on a shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take evening calls and chats about missed grocery deliveries. I started this job after years driving a van, so I know the roads but still need help with the refund rules. I finished secondary school and am a junior agent, slower than the experienced people on mixed payment cases. The evening premium makes my pay higher than most agents, and I use approved AI search every day to find old delivery notes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What else shapes the work decision for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58. My husband Leon works at a print shop; our grown daughters have their own households. We have eleven months of expenses saved and plenty of centres nearby, though few offer my evening premium. I repair bicycles for neighbours on weekends because I like using my hands. I have no settled date or income for leaving full-time work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a quicker route search is useful, but a grocery bag still needs a driver at the right door. I keep the delivery photograph open before approving a refund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my evening calls and higher pay to continue. Eleven months saved lets us handle a van repair without making our daughters part of the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep taking delivery calls and checking AI summaries against the original drop-off photo. In the first year I will replace the money we spent fixing our washing machine from the evening premium before buying another bicycle stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work. The machine in our laundry room gave us more trouble than the one on my screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which mistake did you catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A photo showed the right street name but the wrong building entrance. I knew the corner from my van years and asked the driver to check again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do the bicycle repairs earn money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. I help two neighbours as a favour, and I do not count favours as wages.

I would keep a **driver confirmation** for the wrong entrance.
think: I expect my **evening premium** and calls to continue.
Our **eleven-month reserve** covers a repair without daughter support.
do: Keep handling **grocery complaints** and checking original photos.
Restore **washer-repair savings** from evening pay before buying a stand.

fieldNote: His **night premium** explains high pay despite junior skill.

steps.text: Keep taking grocery delivery calls and checking AI summaries against original photos
Replace washer-repair money from evening premium before buying bicycle stand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the floor that an automatic delivery answer should be counted again when the customer calls back. A closed chat is not proof that dinner reached the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the new review screen, but simpler chats may vanish and take my premium with them. Eleven months saved and nearby jobs help, though a day shift elsewhere could pay much less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I will learn the new AI photo-checker on twenty closed deliveries during paid shifts, comparing the image with the address line. If the manager changes the evening rota, I will compare written weekly pay at three nearby centres before leaving; in the first year after the change, I will apply only where the paid hours cover our rent and regular bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about losing the premium. I like testing a tool; I do not like a shorter pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your husband to cover a cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leon could cover more for a little while, but his print-shop pay is not a reason to accept a worse job. We will compare the full week first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why only closed deliveries?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn where the checker mistakes one apartment entrance for another without sending a live customer to the wrong doorstep. The old cases let me correct my method before a customer waits on me.

say: I would count **repeat delivery calls**, not just closed chats.
I would show **wrong entrances** from the photo check.
think: I expect **simple chats** and my premium could shrink.
I have local choices, but **day wages** may be lower.
do: Learn **AI photo review** on twenty closed cases during paid shifts.
Compare **written weekly wages** at three centres if the evening rota changes.
Apply after cuts only for **paid hours** covering rent and bills.
feel: **Anxious** about the premium, curious about testing.

fieldNote: His new **AI checker** is actual learning beyond daily search.
His husband’s wage is a **short bridge**, not a reason to accept a cut.

steps.text: Learn AI photo checker on twenty closed deliveries during paid shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell agents full thinking AI by 2028 could decide most missed-delivery refunds. Hands-on robots around 2031 are later, but they do not extend a headset job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my evening queue could close, premium and all. Eleven months saved gives us a search, but I am not ready to stop earning because a screen got clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I will ask the centre for written closure dates and price a basic bicycle repair stand only if three neighbours actually book paid repairs. If my calls end in the first year after 2028, I will look for posted paid van-yard roles with weekly wages that cover our rent and bills; the bicycle work would be a second small income, not the mortgage plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about losing the whole queue. Having savings and a useful pair of hands stops me from freezing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you repair enough bicycles?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have only helped neighbours for free so far. I would charge for booked brake and tyre work one Saturday at a time and keep receipts before buying more tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are van yards safe from robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Robots around 2031 might change loading, and general AI could change routing in 2028. I would ask what the paid yard shift actually involves before moving.

say: I would warn **2028 AGI** could settle delivery refunds.
I would separate **2031 robots** from immediate headset risk.
think: I expect my **evening queue** and premium could end.
I still need **paid work** despite eleven months saved.
do: Request **written closure dates** for the evening queue.
Charge for **booked Saturday repairs**, keep receipts before more tools, and price a stand only after three paid bookings.
Seek **posted paid yard shifts** after cuts only with weekly rent-and-bill-covering wages.
feel: **Alarmed** by possible queue closure, still able to act.
S2.quote: Having savings and a useful pair of hands stops me from freezing.
fieldNote: His prior van work supports a **yard search**, not a guaranteed job.
Bicycle repairs become **side income** only with paying bookings.
He knows **2031 robots** may reach loading.

steps.text: Charge booked Saturday repairs; price stand after three paid bookings; keep receipts before further tools
Seek posted paid van-yard shifts after closure with weekly wages covering rent and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years lets us check what actually pays while calls still come in. General AI reaches our desk by 2031; hands-on robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could grow a small repair round without betting our reserve on it. The van yard might also change, so I would keep two modest paths open rather than name one safe trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I will keep the evening queue and take only booked Saturday bicycle repairs, logging hours and parts on paper. If the paid work brings in enough to replace one lost shift for three months running, I will add a second Saturday slot. In the first year after 2031, if call hours fall, I will apply for advertised paid yard work that covers our bills without using the repair money as an assumed wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the calls, but five years lets me see what customers actually pay. A free favour is not a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would leave most of the eleven months alone. I might buy small parts from repair receipts, but not empty the savings account for a van or a workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Leon judge the Saturday work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leon and I would keep one day each week free for family and rest. I do not want a second income that wears me out before Monday calls.

say: I would test **paid repair demand** over several months.
I would distinguish **2031 desk risk** from later robots.
think: I can grow **small repairs** without betting most of our reserve, funding parts from paid receipts.
I will not call a **yard job** permanent shelter.
do: Log **repair hours and parts**; add Saturday slot after three months running replacing one shift, keeping one rest day.
Apply after call cuts for **advertised paid yard work** with bill-covering wages.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test actual receipts.
S3.quote: A free favour is not a business.
fieldNote: The repair threshold uses **three months** of paid bookings, not favours.
He protects **most savings** rather than funding a workshop.
A **rest day** limits the second-income plan.

steps.text: Keep paid evening delivery calls while shifts remain
Log repair hours/parts; add Saturday slot after three months running replacing one shift; keep rest day
Apply after call cuts for advertised paid yard work with bill-covering weekly wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell agents a decade is time to keep earning and test other work in small amounts. General AI reaches calls by 2036 and hands-on robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might want fewer shifts, but I cannot name what income would replace the premium. Eleven months saved gives choice, not an automatic retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I will keep the evening calls and transfer part of each premium to bring the reserve to a full year. I will continue Saturday bicycle repairs only for real bookings, with one day free. In the first year after 2036, if phone hours fall, I will compare paid yard and centre jobs by full weekly wages and keep the repairs small unless their receipts reliably replace a lost shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the far end, fairly steady now. Ten years is useful if the extra income is real rather than a story I tell myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend the whole reserve to stop calls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We have not fixed a retirement income, and the rent arrives monthly. I would keep most of the reserve liquid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They know I enjoy bicycle work, but I would not ask them to fund it. Their households have their own bills.

say: I would compare **full-week wages** over the decade, including whether the evening premium is replaced.
I would separate **2036 calls** from later robots.
think: I cannot name a **replacement premium at 68**.
I see eleven months saved as **choice**, not as enough income to stop working at a fixed date.
do: Keep my **evening calls** and save toward a full year.

Compare **paid jobs** at yards and centres after cuts by full weekly wages.
S4.quote: Eleven months saved gives choice, not an automatic retirement date.
fieldNote: His **one-year reserve target** grows from premium wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the evening queue could vanish before a repair round earns enough. Written closure dates and actual paid yard openings would help. I would need weekly wages that cover the household, not just the promise of a new title.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how many refunds were correct when the customer called back. A delivery photograph can look right until someone who knows the road opens it. I learned that in a van, before I learned it on a screen.

headlineQuote: A delivery photograph can look right until someone who knows the road opens it.
portrait: Adam is a **58-year-old junior agent** with secondary schooling, past van work and a higher evening wage.
He has **eleven months saved**, plentiful nearby centres and grown daughters with separate households.
He uses **approved AI daily** but still needs help with complex refund rules.
He tests **paid bicycle repairs** through bookings while seeking real wage work if the queue shrinks.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could close his higher-paid evening queue before repairs earn enough.
whatWouldHelp: **Written closure dates** and posted yard work with household-covering weekly wages would help.
